problems.source_says: Section 4.2.3 explicitly establishes comparison across different writers, but neither it nor Table 8 specifies whether individual pairwise similarities or aggregated similarities are the observations in the Mann-Whitney analysis. A metric that compares texts does not by itself establish the statistical analysis unit. The definite pair code lacks explicit support; the analysis unit remains unconfirmed and should be null unless additional documentation establishes it.
problems.quote: we analyzed the cosine similarity, semantic similarity, and ROUGE-L [79] scores among HAI-written comments written on the same thread by different participants who share same stance.
problems.locator: PDF pp. 17-19, Section 4.2.3; p. 18, Table 8. Codebook Section 6, Unit (line 101).

problems.source_says: The cosine and ROUGE-L results compare different writers, but the paper does not describe enumeration or aggregation of their similarity scores for the statistical tests. Table 8 reports U for ROUGE-L without observation counts or an explicit analysis-unit definition. Pair is plausible but not verified as the paper's observation unit; retain null rather than assert it. This does not challenge the diversity construct or the transcribed statistics.
problems.quote: We repeated the same analysis for human-written comments in the control group to establish our baseline.
problems.locator: PDF pp. 17-19, Section 4.2.3; p. 18, Table 8. Codebook Section 6, Unit (line 101).

problems.source_says: The supplied codebook defines automated_score as a scoring model for creativity, not every computer-computed text property. Table 3 specifies word count, SMOG readability, politeness markers, named entities, and grammatical-feature extraction; Section 3.2 specifies VADER sentiment and Perspective toxicity. These descriptions support computed output measures but not creativity-scoring models. The measure_detail descriptions are accurate, while the shared automated_score code exceeds the supplied definition. A suitable alternative measure code is not supplied by that vocabulary; leave it null pending a vocabulary decision rather than invent one.
problems.quote: Length Longer in length Word count
problems.locator: PDF p. 9, Table 3; p. 12, Section 3.2, Quantitative Analysis. Codebook Section 6, Measure, automated_score definition (line 98).

problems.source_says: Section 4.2.2 reports computed similarity between each writer's initial draft and final AI-assisted submission: mean semantic similarity 0.67, BERTScore 0.87, and cosine similarity 0.38. These are output-fidelity results relevant to assisted writing, with unit pair and AI available during final production. They can be retained as other/with_ai ancillary measures, not diversity/across_people or after_ai; they have no randomized between-arm effect. The form notes acknowledge omitting them to meet an outcome cap, but no outcome entry preserves these reported results. The number of analyzed pairs and inferential precision are not explicitly established and should remain null.
problems.quote: Similarly, the average high BERTScore of 0.87 indicate that the LLM-rewritten versions closely aligned with the meanings in initial comments.
problems.locator: PDF p. 12, Section 3.2, Quantitative Analysis; pp. 16-17, Section 4.2.2, Content Similarity; p. 18, Figure 6A. Form notes explicitly acknowledge this omission.

problems.field: outcomes: omitted manual coding of opinion distortion
problems.source_says: The authors manually reviewed rewriting outputs and identified 12 instances (12.7%) in which the LLM changed the writer's original opinion. This is an output-based fidelity assessment in addition to the participants' self-reported explanations. It bears on the quality of AI-assisted rewriting and can be retained as ancillary other/with_ai evidence; it is not a comparison of diversity across people. The paper does not establish the denominator, detailed coding protocol, or whether all these rewrites were accepted as final submissions, so those details remain null. The form notes acknowledge the omission, but the count and percentage are absent from the outcome entries.
problems.quote: Upon manual review, we identified 12 instances (12.7%) where LLM changed people’s original opinion when rewriting their comments constructively—especially when the views were in a spectrum.
problems.locator: PDF p. 19, Section 4.2.4, Editing. Form notes explicitly acknowledge this omission.

summary: Criterion 3 holds because the paper computes similarity across different participants' final comments. The reported numbers match the PDF, but two analysis-unit codes and the automated_score labels lack support under the supplied definitions, and two output-fidelity analyses are absent from the outcome entries.
